title: First steps in Python
overview: This is the first folder of the Software Engineering Track and a first Python program. After months of C, Python feels very light: there is no `main`, no `#include`, no semicolons and no compiling. You write a line and the interpreter runs it from top to bottom.

concepts.explain: Python reads the file and runs each line in order. There is no compile step and no `main()` function you must write.
`print` writes its arguments and then adds a newline by itself, so you don't need to type `\n` as you do in C's `printf`.
Text goes inside single or double quotes. Both kinds work the same way.
From a terminal, type `python first.py`. The output shows up right away.

files.title: Hello World in Python
files.what: The classic first program. It checks that Python is installed and that you can run a script.
steps: `print("Hello World")` is the only line in the file.
Python passes the string to `print`, which writes it and then a newline.
The script ends when there are no more lines. There is no `return 0`.
files.output_note: You should see exactly one line: `Hello World`.
files.watch_out: Python 3 needs the brackets: `print "Hello"` (without them) is Python 2 syntax and raises a SyntaxError.

check.q: What is the C line that does the same thing, and what does Python add for you?
check.a: `printf("Hello World\n");`. Python's `print` adds the newline for you.

recap: Python runs the file from top to bottom. There is no `main` and no compiling.
`print()` adds a newline at the end by itself.
Strings can use single or double quotes.

check_yourself.q: Name two things a C Hello World needs that the Python one does not.
check_yourself.a: Any two of these: `#include <stdio.h>`, a `main` function, semicolons, `return 0`, a compile step.

check_yourself.q: How many lines does `print("a"); print("b")` print?
check_yourself.a: Two, because each `print` ends with its own newline.

body: You have spent a year with C and then C++: headers, a `main`, a type for every variable, a semicolon on every line, braces round every block, and a compiler that refuses to build the program until all of that is right.
Python drops nearly all of it. Here is the same program - print one line of text - in both languages, side by side.

Four lines become one, and nothing is missing. There is no header to include, because `print` is always there. There is no `main`: Python starts at the first line of the file and runs down to the last one. There is no `return 0` and no build step - you type `python first.py` and it runs.
`print` is not `printf`. It has no format specifiers: you hand it the things you want printed and it works out how to show them. It also adds the newline for you, which is why the `\n` disappeared.

Variables need no type. You do not write `int n;` - you write `n = 5`, and Python decides that `n` is a whole number. Write `n = "five"` on the next line and it is now text. Nothing has to be declared before it is used.
intro.snippet:
n = 5
name = "Rafi"
print(name, "has", n, "books")
# Rafi has 5 books

body: Braces are gone too, and this is the one change that trips people up. In C, indentation was politeness and `{ }` decided what belonged to the `if`. In Python, indentation **is** the syntax. A line ending in a colon opens a block, and everything indented under it belongs to that block.
Four spaces is the usual step. Mixing tabs and spaces, or indenting by different amounts inside one block, is an error and not a matter of taste.

Input works differently in a way worth learning on day one. `scanf("%d", &n)` told C that the next thing is a number. `input()` makes no such promise: it reads one line and gives you **text**, always. If you want a number, you convert it yourself with `int()` or `float()`.
Forget the conversion and nothing crashes - you get a wrong answer, which is worse. With the two lines `3` and `4` typed in:
intro.trace:
a = input()        a = int(input())
b = input()        b = int(input())
print(a + b)       print(a + b)

34                 7
(text joined)      (numbers added)

body: **One caution to carry over from C.** In C, `7 / 2` with two ints gave 3, because division between whole numbers threw the remainder away. In Python, `/` always produces a decimal: `7 / 2` is `3.5`, and `6 / 2` is `3.0`, not `3`. The C-style division is spelled `//`, so `7 // 2` is 3. Use `//` whenever you want a whole number - counting halves, splitting into groups, taking a middle index. One more difference: `//` rounds **down**, so `-7 // 2` is `-4`, while C's `/` gave `-3`.

Why any of this is worth your time: the same idea takes a third of the lines, there is no compile step, so testing a thought costs seconds. The price is that the compiler no longer checks your types - a mistake that C would have refused to build now waits quietly until that line runs.
The file below is a one-line Hello World. Run it, see the output, and you know your Python installation works.
